title: The Quiet Work of Rope
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The rope snapped with a sound like somebody cracking a whip across the shore.

I saw Maui's hand jerk backward. The mooring post shuddered. A boat that had been safely tucked against the Tideglass landing swung toward the rocks, and the two children sitting inside it screamed.

"Maui!"

He was already moving.

He caught the bow with his hook before the boat could strike the stone. His feet planted in the wet sand, knees bent, and for a moment the whole dock seemed to strain against him. Then Fen reached the line, dragged it through the remaining ring, and tied off the boat while I helped the children onto the steps.

They were frightened. They were unhurt.

Maui was still smiling when I turned toward him.

"See?" he said. "Everyone's fine."

His left hand was bleeding.

"Show me."

"It's a scratch."

"Maui."

He held it up. There was a raw stripe across the base of his palm, deeper at one end where the rope had caught. He flexed his fingers and tried to hide the wince under a grin.

"Hero's scratch."

"Well, the hero is going to sit down."

Fen looked at the broken line and swore softly.

"That shouldn't have given way."

I checked the end. One part was frayed, but a second section looked almost polished. The strand had been rubbing against the underside of the landing, where a nail had shifted during the recent repairs.

"Maintenance failure," I said.

Fen nodded.

"Not a monster?"

Maui looked mildly offended.

"I could still fight one."

"Try fighting a clean bandage first."

The clinic didn't open until noon, but Katara had left an emergency kit in the public storage cabinet. I made Maui sit on an overturned crate while I cleaned the cut. He watched with an expression of tremendous patience that lasted perhaps thirty seconds.

"I could heal faster as a hawk."

"Do hawks have hands?"

"Not technically."

"Then stay as you are."

He examined the wound over my shoulder.

"I've had worse."

"I believe you."

"Much worse."

"Still believe you."

"That time with the eel—"

"If you tell me this cut is nothing compared to an eel, I am going to make the bandage extremely decorative."

He shut his mouth.

Fen took the broken line to Tamsin's workshop. The children went home with Mara, who offered bread and a stern lecture about staying seated while docking. By the time I finished the bandage, the tide had begun to turn.

Maui reached for his hook.

"No," I said.

He stared at me.

"No?"

"Not until we know whether that hand needs proper treatment. And not until somebody else examines the rest of the moorings."

"I can inspect them."

"I know you can. That's not the problem."

"Then what is?"

I wanted to say that he was exhausting. I wanted to say that I couldn't bear the thought of him being hurt again, because the sight of blood on his hand had made something awful open inside my chest.

Neither would explain why the dock had failed.

"The problem," I said carefully, "is that everyone assumes you're the solution to every emergency. Even you."

For a long moment he said nothing.

Then he looked toward the children disappearing into the square.

"They were scared."

"I know."

"And I could help."

"You did help. Now other people get to help too."

He looked down at the bandage.

"Doesn't feel right."

That was the most honest thing he'd said all morning.

At Tamsin's workshop, Fen showed us three knots with different jobs. One held under steady weight, one could be untied after a sudden pull, and the third was designed so a damaged line could be replaced without anyone putting a hand where the load would crush it.

I got the first one wrong twice.

Maui got it right immediately, then tried to demonstrate with his injured hand.

Mini Maui appeared at his wrist and performed an entire play about a heroic injured hand. It ended with the miniature collapsing dramatically beside a rope.

"I know," Maui said. "I'm suffering."

"You're showing off," I said.

"Two things can be true."

Fen pulled the line toward them and pointed to the section that would carry the actual load. Maui leaned closer, interested despite himself. He'd tied enough lines in his life to make the motions look effortless, but he was watching how Fen tested this particular wet rope.

"Is this how all of you pass the time?" he asked. "Inventing ways to make a demigod feel inadequate?"

"Mostly we repair the damage caused by people who never check their knots."

Maui looked wounded. Then he grinned and offered his uninjured hand.

"Fine. Tell me what the legendary Maui has to do to pass your tiny rope exam."

He listened to the answer. His hand was shaking by the end, partly from the cut and partly from how determined he was not to be the person who made the next boat unsafe. The grin stayed. So did the effort.

Fen slapped the rope away.

"Use the other one."

"You're very demanding for a person teaching knots."

"You're very loud for somebody who hasn't paid the repair bill."

Maui blinked.

"There's a bill?"

"There is always a bill."

Fen pointed to the ledger on the wall. Rope cost money. Nails cost money. Tamsin's time cost money. So did replacement planks. The Lanternweald's dock fees paid for some things, but not everything, and the people who kept boats floating weren't decorative figures in somebody else's epic.

We all looked at the ledger.

Two weeks of repairs had nearly emptied the landing fund.

"Why didn't you tell us?" I asked.

"Because half the village offers to help for free and the other half feels guilty about not being able to," Fen said. "I need the tools paid for. I don't need a parade."

Maui was quiet.

I wondered whether he was considering selling a legend to cover the price of nails.

Instead he asked, "How much for the rope?"

Fen named an amount.

"I can pay some," Maui said.

"You don't owe the whole dock because you were here when it failed."

"I know. But I use it."

Fen looked surprised.

"That's different."

I spent the afternoon helping inspect the mooring points. We marked each one with colored thread, not to rank them but to show which were safe, which needed maintenance, and which were closed until tested. Pip offered to translate the signs for travelers who couldn't read the Lanternweald script. Toph arrived and tapped the planks with her heel.

"Wood's talking," she announced.

"Does it have good news?" I asked.

"Some of it's begging to be replaced."

She marked two supports we'd missed.

Maui hated staying on the bench. He was especially offended when a small child offered him a cup of water and called him brave for sitting still.

"That was sarcastic," he said after the child left.

"That was generous."

"You're enjoying this."

"Immensely."

By sunset the dock was closed, the replacement list was posted, and nobody had suffered another injury.

I found Maui alone at the end of the cove. He held a short length of spare rope in his good hand, turning it over as if it were a puzzle.

"Fen taught me something," he said.

"A knot?"

"No. Well, yes. But something else." He pulled one loop through another. "When I was younger, people always wanted proof I was strong. Then when I became strong, they wanted proof I could do anything. I got used to being the person nobody had to ask."

I sat beside him.

"Does it frighten you to be asked to stop?"

He took a long time to answer.

"It frightens me that if I stop, you might discover you never needed me."

The words made me ache.

"Maui."

He looked at me with an openness so unlike his stage voice that I barely recognized it.

"I need you," I said. "But not because you can hold a boat against the sea. I need the person who remembered I hate my tea too sweet. The one who painted a crab on a safety sign and then made sure it was the correct kind of crab."

"It is a very accurate crab."

"The most accurate."

He laughed once.

"I need you to tell me when you're scared," I continued. "And I need you to let somebody else hold a rope when you're hurt."

He looked at his bandage.

"Even if they're bad at knots?"

"Especially then. They can learn."

He looped his good arm around my shoulders. I leaned against him. His cheek brushed my hair, warm from the sun, and the smell of salt and timber rose between us.

"I could teach you the next knot," he murmured.

"Tomorrow. Tonight you're coming home."

"Bossy."

"You like it."

"Terribly."

He kissed me, slow enough that I could feel his smile become something gentler. We went home before the tide rose.

The following morning, the broken mooring was still broken. The ledger still needed funds. But Fen had drawn a new maintenance rota, Tamsin had priced the supplies, and Maui had signed up for a shift he could do with one hand.

Nobody owed him applause.

He seemed relieved.
